payload.reason: Supplier cut allocation 40% — DDR5 wafer starts reallocated to HBM
payload.plain: Our main memory supplier just said they will ship 40% less than we ordered. We are 4,608 memory modules short, and the factory needs them in 11 days. Every minute without a decision costs about $1,240 in idle line time and late-delivery penalties — roughly $1.8M a day.

payload.text: Allocation alert confirmed and normalised. Our qualified primary RDIMM is short against the AI-SRV-G4 build and the supplier has reallocated wafer starts to HBM, so this is a supply decision, not a price negotiation. Room order: Sourcing brings alternates, Engineering qualifies them against the platform QVL and may block, Quality screens any non-franchised offer for authenticity, then a human approves. 4 candidates to work through.
payload.plain: our main memory supplier will ship far less than we ordered, the factory needs the parts in days, and every minute we spend deciding costs us idle-line and late-delivery money.

sources.title: DDR5 RDIMM server module contract pricing — quarterly trend
sources.snippet: Server DRAM contract prices continued to climb quarter over quarter as suppliers reallocated wafer capacity toward HBM. 64GB DDR5-4800 RDIMM modules saw the steepest move in the conventional server segment, with spot quotes running well above contract.

sources.title: Spot market quotes, 64GB DDR5-4800 RDIMM
sources.snippet: Spot offers for 64GB DDR5-4800 registered modules widened against contract pricing, with broker inventory commanding a premium. Buyers report quote validity windows shortening to days.

sources.title: Memory market outlook — conventional DRAM under HBM squeeze
sources.snippet: Every wafer moved to HBM removes several times its area of conventional DDR5 supply. Analysts expect server DDR5 tightness to persist while HBM qualification ramps absorb leading-edge capacity.

payload.plain: Found 3 sources on what modules are selling for.

sources.title: Distributor stock and quoted lead times — DDR5 RDIMM
sources.snippet: Authorised distribution shows limited on-hand quantity for 64GB DDR5-4800 RDIMM with factory lead times quoted in multiples of weeks. Backorder positions are being accepted without firm delivery commitment.

sources.title: Server memory availability and allocation status
sources.snippet: Several registered DDR5 server module lines show no stock with scheduled factory deliveries. Where stock exists it is in quantities below typical cluster build volumes.

payload.plain: Found 2 sources on who has stock and how long delivery takes.

payload.label: Scanning allocation and supply news
payload.plain: Searching the open market right now for prices, who has stock, and news about the shortage.

sources.title: Memory suppliers place server DRAM customers on allocation
sources.snippet: Suppliers have notified server and ODM customers of reduced allocation on conventional DDR5 server memory as capacity shifts toward high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators. Affected buyers are being asked to requalify alternate module sources.

sources.title: HBM capacity expansion pressures conventional DRAM output
sources.snippet: HBM production consumes substantially more wafer area per bit than conventional DRAM, so the AI-driven HBM ramp directly reduces available DDR5 bit supply. Server builders report allocation cuts and extended lead times.

sources.title: Counterfeit and remarked server memory resurfaces in shortage conditions
sources.snippet: Shortage conditions historically correlate with a rise in remarked and counterfeit memory modules entering the independent distribution channel. Buyers are advised to verify top markings and lot codes against manufacturer references before acceptance.

payload.plain: Found 3 sources on why supply is short.

payload.text: Decoded the at-risk part number and pulled cross-vendor equivalents in 0.23ms, then checked pricing, distributor stock and allocation news. 4 offers on the table. Cheapest is Micron (offered via broker — Pacific Rim Components Ltd., HK) MTC20F2085S1RC48BA1 at $152.75 a module, 0 week(s) out — same specification on paper, and I want it considered seriously because the delta across the full quantity is real money. The safe option is V-color Technology TRA564G48D436O at $186.4, in stock at a franchised distributor.
payload.plain: I found several replacements. The cheapest looks identical on the datasheet; the dearest one is in stock with full paperwork. Engineering's call now — I am not claiming any of these is approved.

The cheapest offer — about $209,000 less across the whole order, and the spec sheet is an exact match. But this supplier's memory was never actually tested in this server. It fits on paper and nobody has ever run 24 of them in one machine at full load. Could take the cluster down.

payload.text: Ran the platform QVL lookup on all 4 candidates. V-color Technology TRA564G48D436O is BLOCKED — Not on platform QVL for AI-SRV-G4 (QVL-G4-2026.08-rev-D). Spec-compatible on all 5 platform requirements MATCH (64 / 4800 / 2Rx4 / RDIMM / 1.1V), but EVAL-G4-0412 is incomplete — incomplete. I want to be precise about why I am blocking the cheapest option, because it will look unreasonable: it matches every platform requirement. It is still blocked. The QVL is a record of what has been TESTED in this machine, not a list of what fits. Spec-compatible is not qualified. Nobody has run a full chassis of these at thermal load, and discovering the problem during a customer's burn-in is how we lose the cluster and the contract.  Qualified and available to us: Micron (offered via broker — Pacific Rim Components Ltd., HK) MTC20F2085S1RC48BA1, Samsung Semiconductor M321R8GA0BB0-CQK, SK hynix HMCG94MEBRA109N.
payload.plain: the cheapest memory was never tested in this server, so I will not let it into the build. These other parts were tested, and we should buy one of them. One caveat for Quality: the QVL clears a part NUMBER. It says nothing about whether a particular seller's units are genuine.

payload.plain: Closest match in 0.19ms: Broker unit — REMARKED, claims -CQK at 88% similarity.

payload.text: Rejecting the broker lot from Open-market broker, non-franchised — ex-stock Hong Kong. Lot PRC-24817 — COUNTERFEIT — REMARKED MODULE. 6 independent marking failures: (1) F1 — expected D8BNJ, observed D8BQK; (2) F2 — expected valid YYWW, not earlier than 2024-W18 (PCB rev E2 first build), observed sub-lot A = 2341 (2023 week 41); sub-lot B = 2354 (week 54 does not exist); (3) F3 — expected laser-etched, observed ink-overprint-on-abraded-surface; (4) F4 — expected micron-laser-v3, pitch 0.92mm, observed generic-sans, pitch 1.05mm; (5) F5 — expected 8 hex chars within an issued range, plus a readable DataMatrix, observed serial 00000000 (outside every issued range), DataMatrix absent; (6) F6 — expected manufacturer, location, date, serial and part number all populated and consistent, observed moduleManufacturerJep106 = 0x2C (correct) but location 0x00, date 0000, serial 00000000 all blank. Top-marking matches Broker unit — REMARKED, claims -CQK at 0.88, against only 0.81 to the genuine reference. Module-level remark: the packages were re-labelled on an already-assembled module, so the die origin is unknown and unverifiable. Matched in 0.19ms, on-device. Note that this part number PASSED Engineering's qualification check — that is exactly the point. Qualification and authenticity are independent, and the part being on the QVL is what makes a remarked unit worth faking.
payload.plain: A middleman offered us thousands of the exact part we are short of, immediately, at 29% below our normal price. The markings on the chips were sanded off and reprinted. These are not the part they claim to be, and we cannot tell what is actually inside them. The code printed on the chips is not the code this exact part uses. The dates do not add up. One batch says the chips are older than the board they are mounted on. The other batch has a date that cannot exist. The original markings were sanded off and new ones printed on top. You can see the scratch marks. The lettering is the wrong font and the wrong size. There is no serial number the manufacturer can look up, and the square tracking code is missing entirely. Every stick we checked had the same blank serial. The stick's internal data chip says 'Micron' but has no record of where or when it was actually made. Those details are written at the factory, so their absence means this stick did not come off that factory's line.

payload.text: Recommendation: Samsung Semiconductor M321R8GA0BB0-CQK at $231.8 a module, 1 week(s) from Franchised distributor — 5,100 pcs ex-stock, ARO 5 working days. It is on the platform QVL, it is a drop-in module replacement with no die substitution and no board change, and it arrives inside the build window. Rejections: TRA564G48D436O: not qualified on this platform; MTC20F2085S1RC48BA1: qualified part number, counterfeit units; HMCG94MEBRA109N: qualified, but 14 weeks misses the build.
payload.plain: one option is both tested in this server and genuinely available in time. The cheap one was never tested, and the fast cheap one was fake. Hand it to a human to approve.

payload.plain: Approve the tested, in-stock replacement: 4,608 modules for $1,068,134.4, arriving in about 1 week(s). It looks more expensive than the middleman's offer — but that offer would have meant scrapping the lot and rebuilding the servers, so this decision is the cheaper one.
A human approved the purchase. This is the only decision the agents did not make on their own.
